claims.claim: Socialization is the process whereby an individual learns to adjust to a group or society and behave in a manner approved by it; most social scientists treat it as the whole process of learning throughout the life course.
Socialization is how people learn to function successfully in their social worlds: learning to use the objects of material culture and adopting the beliefs, values, and norms of nonmaterial culture.

Socialization is critical both to individuals and to the societies in which they live; a society perpetuates itself by teaching its way of life to new members, and without socialization people literally have no self.
Family is the first agent of socialization; peer groups, schools, workplaces, and the media are additional agents that communicate expectations and reinforce norms.
Charles Cooley asserted that people's self-understanding is constructed in part by their perception of how others view them, a process he termed the looking-glass self.
George Herbert Mead studied the self as a person's distinct identity developed through social interaction; through socialization people learn to view themselves through the eyes of others.
Socialization is a lifelong process, not a one-time event; age-related transition points such as becoming school age, entering the workforce, or retiring require socialization into a new role.

Resocialization is the process in which old behaviors that were helpful in a previous role are removed because they are no longer of use; it is necessary when a person moves to a senior care center, goes to boarding school, or serves a prison sentence, and is typically more stressful than ordinary socialization.
Anticipatory socialization is the preparation for future life roles, such as a couple cohabitating before marriage or soon-to-be parents reading infant-care books.

Genetics and hormones play an important role in human behavior, but sociology's larger concern is the effect of society on behavior; socialization shapes people without stamping them once and for all.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How much does socialization determine who a person becomes?
positions: Nature emphasis: temperament, interests, and talents are set before birth; twin studies point to genetic roots of behavior (OpenStax 5.2).
Nurture emphasis: who we are results from the relationships and caring that surround us; without socialization we have no self (OpenStax 5.2).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both sides and lands on the sociological middle: socialization is essential and lifelong, but biology also plays a role, so socialization shapes without fully determining. This is stated simply as the honest note, not argued in depth.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Do peers or parents have more influence during adolescence?
positions: Friendships rank high in adolescents' priorities (OpenStax 5.3).
Studies show parental influence balances the priority given to friendships (OpenStax 5.3).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson treats agents as layered rather than competing: peers deliver new lessons, while family influence persists, which is why no single agent decides a person.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Sociology 3e, 5.1 Theories of Self-Development
sourceRecords.notes: Read via an Internet Archive capture of the canonical OpenStax URL (web.archive.org/web/2025). Supports Cooley's looking-glass self (self-understanding built partly from perceived views of others) and Mead's self (distinct identity developed through social interaction; viewing oneself through others' eyes).

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Sociology 3e, 5.2 Why Socialization Matters
sourceRecords.notes: Read via an Internet Archive capture of the canonical OpenStax URL (web.archive.org/web/2025). Supports socialization as critical to individuals and societies, society perpetuating itself by teaching its way of life, 'without socialization we literally have no self', the nature-versus-nurture discussion (genetics and hormones play a role), and the three-theory perspectives (functionalist, conflict, interactionist).

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Sociology 3e, 5.3 Agents of Socialization
sourceRecords.notes: Read via an Internet Archive capture of the canonical OpenStax URL (web.archive.org/web/2025). Supports family as the first agent, peer groups as adolescents' first major socialization outside the family (with parental influence balancing peer priorities), schools/workplaces/government as formal institutions, and media distributing impersonal messages about beliefs, values, and norms.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Sociology 3e, 5.4 Socialization Across the Life Course
sourceRecords.notes: Read via an Internet Archive capture of the canonical OpenStax URL (web.archive.org/web/2025). Supports socialization as a lifelong process ('not stamped by some socialization machine'), age-related transition points (school age, workforce entry, retirement), resocialization (removal of old behaviors no longer of use; senior care center, boarding school, prison; typically more stressful), and anticipatory socialization (cohabitation before marriage, reading infant-care books).
